# The Unlit Hours

Every evening now, the sun sets twice. First the real sunset—orange bleeding to violet over the western horizon—and then, half an hour later, the second sunset, when the accumulated glow of billions of lamps bounces off the atmosphere and turns the whole sky a sodium orange. Photographs taken from orbit show our civilization for what it has become: a web of light. Cities glow like fever charts, highways string themselves into luminous threads between them, fishing fleets burn like galaxies off the coasts of Japan and Argentina. From up there, human history looks like a story about pushing back the dark.

For almost all of that history, however, night was not something to push back against. It was simply the second half of existence, governed by its own physics, its own economy, its own rules of behavior. The conquest of darkness is one of the great triumphs of technology—and also one of the least examined. We tallied up everything we gained from abolishing the night and forgot to ask what we lost. The losses turn out to be stranger and larger than anyone expected: pieces of our biology, an entire ecological order, and a relationship with the sky that every generation of humans before us held in common.

## First Sleep

Begin with how completely the old darkness closed in. When the sun went down in a village of five hundred years ago, the world didn't dim—it evaporated. Visual range shrank to the radius of a single flame. Travel became genuinely dangerous, not just inconvenient, so roads emptied and gates were barred. The medieval English enforced a curfew whose name preserves the whole logic: *couvre-feu*, cover-fire, a bell rung at nightfall telling households to bank their hearths so stray embers wouldn't find the thatch.

Light inside the house was a scarce commodity with an almost unbearable price structure. Beeswax candles belonged to churches and the rich. Tallow candles—rendered animal fat—smoked, guttered, and filled rooms with a rancid smell; lighting several at once marked you as extravagant, which is presumably where we got our phrase about burning the candle at both ends. Most families made do with rushlights: dried rushes whose pith had been dipped in kitchen grease. They were wonderfully cheap and horribly brief—a rushlight burned for fifteen minutes or so, which meant light came in parsimonious installments, ignited only when someone needed to find something or finish a chore, and pinched out the instant the task was done.

But here is where the old night gets strange. Because sleep researchers and historians started paying attention, we now know that our ancestors did not experience the night as one long sleep interrupted by nothing. A few decades ago, the historian Roger Ekirch went looking through diaries, court records, medical texts, and prayer manuals stretching back centuries, and found the same thing everywhere: references to the "first sleep" and the "second sleep," treated as ordinary and unremarkable. French sources speak of the *premier sommeil*, Italian ones of the *primo sonno*. Between the two sleeps lay an interval—an hour, sometimes two—that people called "the watch." During it, they got up. They stoked the fire, tended animals, knitted, read by rushlight, prayed, made love, visited neighbors, or simply lay awake thinking, in what must have been one of the rare stretches of genuinely private consciousness in a crowded preindustrial life.

Laboratory work eventually confirmed that this wasn't quaint habit but latent biology. When volunteers were kept in long, natural darkness—fourteen hours a night, mimicking a winter evening before lamps—their sleep organized itself into two distinct phases with a period of quiet, oddly contented wakefulness in the middle. Given the chance, the body remembers the watch.

That old darkness was also psychologically generative. With sight starved of data, the imagination filled the vacuum. This is the simple ecological explanation for why every preindustrial culture populated the dark so densely—with ghosts, revenants, fairies, demons. Even the word *nightmare* carries the fossil: the *mara*, a spirit believed to sit on the chest of sleepers and crush the breath out of them. The dark wasn't empty, so it couldn't stay empty. It teemed.

## The Conquest

The counterattack came slowly and then all at once. In 1667, Paris installed lanterns at regular intervals along its streets—one of the first systematic attempts to extend civic order into the hours after dark—and helped earn the city its title, *la Ville Lumière*, the City of Light, an irony considering the moniker predates electricity by two centuries. Gas lighting arrived in London in the early 1800s and changed the arithmetic entirely: for the first time, streets could be brightly lit mile after mile, shops could put merchandise in windows that worked all night as advertisements, and factories could run through the small hours with something approaching daylight efficiency. The night shift was invented, and with it a new assumption—that production, like water, should flow continuously.

Edison's practical incandescent bulb in 1879, and the power stations that followed, finished the job in the cities. Rural electrification extended it outward through the twentieth century until darkness survived mainly as an accident of geography. Today the process has essentially run to completion across the developed world, and it is completing itself elsewhere at astonishing speed: parts of India, East Africa, and Southeast Asia that lacked reliable electricity a generation ago now blaze at night as thoroughly as Kansas.

One small inversion of this story deserves notice, if only because it reveals what everyone unconsciously knows. During the World Wars, cities subjected themselves to blackout—dousing or hooding every light—and citizens described the result with a mixture of dread and awe. The blacked-out metropolis at night was dangerous, yes, but also unprecedented: a Modern city returned, wholesale, to conditions our species knew for a hundred thousand years. People hated it. And people also stood in the streets looking up, seeing stars over Piccadilly for the first time in their lives.

## What the Stars Said

That glimpse points to the largest casualty of the war on darkness: the sky itself.

A comprehensive atlas published in 2016 calculated that more than 80 percent of humanity now lives under light-polluted skies. One-third of people alive—including, remarkably, 60 percent of Europeans and nearly 80 percent of North Americans—cannot see the Milky Way from where they live. Think about that number. The Milky Way. The pale river of stars that every human who ever lived looked upon, that every mythology is partially built from, that every previous generation considered simply *the sky*—is now hidden from most members of our species by a veil of our own making.

Before we buried it, the night sky was our original library, calendar, and church. The Pleiades told farmers when to plant and when to expect rain on four continents. The heliacal rise of Sirius announced the Nile flood. Polaris, hanging almost motionless, let sailors fix their latitude and cross open ocean; its altitude above the horizon equals your latitude north, an equation written in the heavens and legible to anyone patient enough to measure it. Temples and tomb-shafts were aimed at solstice risings with a precision that still humbles surveyors. Astronomy—which was, for most of recorded history, just careful noticing—was the most democratic science conceivable: every instrument required was attached to your own neck.

There is a version of enchantment available nowhere else in this. The light entering your eye from the Andromeda Galaxy left it two and a half million years ago, before our genus existed. Every watcher of that faint smudge—all the way back—is receiving the same ancient message. Even Uranus, spotted by telescope in 1781, moved Keats to imagine "some watcher of the skies / When a new planet swims into his ken." All of that imaginative traffic ran through a channel that has now closed, silently and without ceremony, for eight out of ten of us.

And one eerie footnote. The darkness of the night sky is not trivially explained; if the universe were static and infinitely old and infinitely large, every direction you looked would terminate on the surface of a star, and the sky would blaze. Edgar Allan Poe, in his strangest and last essay, *Eureka*, intuited the answer ahead of the physicists: the darkness means the light hasn't arrived yet—because the universe is young. The dark overhead is itself a piece of cosmological evidence. Turn off the lights, and you can read a proof about the origin of time with your naked eye. Most of us can't even see the page.

## The Biology of Light Spill

The costs don't stop at the horizon line; they run straight into the body.

Vision scientists discovered not long ago that humans possess a third kind of photoreceptor, alongside rods and cones—not for seeing images but for measuring ambient brightness, tuned exquisitely to blue wavelengths: exactly the color of morning sky and exactly the color of most screens and LEDs. Shine that spectrum at your eyes in the evening and the measurement comes back "daytime," instructing the brain to withhold melatonin, delaying and shallowing sleep. Light pollution doesn't just hide the stars outside; it recreates noon indoors, where the pineal gland has no jurisdiction.

The epidemiological shadow of circadian disruption is broad. Regulators classify night-shift work involving circadian disruption as a probable human carcinogen, based largely on studies of long-term shift workers showing elevated risks of breast and prostate cancers—a suspected mechanism running through chronic melatonin suppression. Meanwhile, a quieter revelation connects back to Ekirch: countless people wake at three in the morning, panic that something is wrong with them, lie anxious for an hour, and conclude they suffer from insomnia. For many of them, nothing is wrong at all. Their compressed, single-block sleep has ended at the historically normal seam. They're experiencing the watch—except alone, in the dark, wondering why they feel broken. Some sleep therapists now treat such patients simply by telling them the history. The anxiety often dissolves on contact with context.

Wildlife pays a higher price, because most animals were never consulted about the abolition of night. Around half of known vertebrate species and a far greater share of insects are nocturnal; for them, light pollution isn't aesthetic degradation—it's habitat destruction measured in lumens. Sea turtle hatchlings evolved to scramble toward the brighter seaward horizon moonlight paints on the waves; beachfront hotels repoint them inland, toward parking lots and roads, in broad(lit) daylight. Hundreds of thousands of migrating songbirds, navigating by stars they increasingly cannot detect, funnel into glass towers outlined in decorative light on stormy migration nights; after researchers showed that New York's Tribute in Light was circling and trapping enormous numbers of birds on any given night of operation, the installation's operators agreed to switch off the beams whenever counts spiked. Fireflies advertise mates in the only language they have—flashes—and suburban glow renders love letters illegible. Even corals, spawning in synchrony timed to the moon, miss their appointments near illuminated coastlines.

## Giving Back the Night

None of this requires despairing, because none of it is irreversible. Darkness, unlike so many things we've degraded, refills the moment you stop dispelling it.

Some places understood this early. Flagstaff, Arizona, watching over the observatory where Pluto was discovered, passed lighting ordinances in 1958 and in 2001 became the world's first officially designated Dark Sky City—its downtown streets lit warm and low and fully shielded, pointing luminance at the pavement instead of the clouds. Quebec's Mont-Mégantic became the world's first Dark Sky Reserve, a federation of towns collectively dimming themselves enough that a professional observatory operates inside them. There are now dozens of such reserves and well over two hundred certified dark-sky places worldwide, and the movement's tricks are almost embarrassingly inexpensive: full cutoff fixtures, timers, motion sensors, and warm-colored lamps that happen to be less attractive to insects and less disruptive to wildlife as a bonus. Light only what needs lighting, only when it needs lighting, only as bright as necessary—the dark-sky movement's entire manifesto fits on an index card.

Individuals command surprising leverage too. A porch light burning on a sensor beats a floodlight burning all night; glare, it turns out, helps neither neighbors nor police, since pools of brightness ringed by deep shadow aid concealment as much as detection. Outdoor fixtures on 2200-kelvin amber bulbs spare the moths and preserve something for the neighbors' retinas. And indoors, dimming and warming the lights after sunset is a small courtesy to your own pineal gland.

## Keeping Some of the Dark

It's worth stepping back, finally, to ask what we would even be keeping darkness *for*.

Not nostalgia, exactly—or not only. Consider what the dark actually is: not an absence but a condition, the condition in which certain things exist and become perceptible. Your own night vision takes the better part of forty minutes to come online fully; that's why astronomers guard their adaptation with red flashlights. Only in the dark do the faintest objects appear, and only in the dark, too, do hearing and attention redistribute—the owl's competence is latent in all of us. Darkness is where half the planet's living things carry out their lives. On those grounds alone, it ought to be regarded the way we regard wetlands: as habitat, worthy of protection, not merely a resource awaiting conversion to a brighter purpose.

And consider what's folded inside it. The night sky is the single oldest continuous possession of our species—the one spectacle thatCro-Magnon child, Egyptian priest, Mongol herdsman, and Victorian poet all attended without translation. Within a handful of generations, we suspended that inheritance for most of our descendants. There's something quietly melancholy in the thought that the stars haven't changed—they are exactly where Keats's watcher found Uranus swimming—but the audience has been mostly dismissed. The door is unlocked; we've merely stopped going through it.

So here is the modest proposal, the essay reduced to one instruction: sometime in the next year, drive beyond the glowing edge of a city—two hours is usually enough—and stop somewhere flat on a moonless night. Give your eyes the forty minutes they ask for, resisting the phone, whose screen will erase in seconds everything the wait earns. Watch the faint cloud of the Milky Way condense out of the background as your pupils drink up the last photons: ten thousand suns arranged in a river, more stars than you can resolve, the same view your ancestors fell asleep beneath at the bottom of the first sleep, about to wake for the watch.

It doesn't require accepting any mystical doctrine to find the experience altering. You will be standing in the only cathedral that admits everyone, receiving light older than continents, participating in the most universal ritual there has ever been. The porch light will still work tomorrow.

Leave it off tonight instead. The sky has been talking the whole time.
